title: Question 1.1
statement_text: What are the unavoidable induced subgraphs of graphs with large treewidth?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. The question asks for a list of graph families such that every graph of sufficiently large treewidth contains a large member of one of them as an induced subgraph, analogous to the grid theorem. For subgraphs and minors the answer is Robertson and Seymour's theorem: every graph of large treewidth contains a subdivision of a large $r\times r$ wall $W_{r\times r}$ (the $r$-by-$r$ hexagonal grid) as a subgraph. For induced subgraphs the answer must include the basic obstructions: complete graphs, complete bipartite graphs $K_{t,t}$, subdivisions of walls, and line graphs of subdivisions of walls. These are not enough, as shown by non-basic obstructions such as the Pohoata–Davies graphs, occultations and layered wheels. In all of them large treewidth comes with a large complete minor, and the first two even have large complete bipartite induced minors. Here $G$ has an induced minor isomorphic to $H$ if there are pairwise disjoint connected induced subgraphs (branch sets) $G_v$, $v\in V(H)$, such that $G_u$ and $G_v$ are joined by an edge exactly when $uv\in E(H)$. This question is the central goal of the authors' series of papers on induced subgraphs and tree decompositions. In this paper they characterize the unavoidable induced subgraphs of graphs with a large complete bipartite induced minor. Such a graph either has a large wall as an induced minor or contains a large constellation: a graph with a stable set $S$ such that every component of the rest is a path and every vertex of $S$ has a neighbour in each of these paths. They also show that large constellations contain basic obstructions or one of two highly structured types of constellations (generalizing occultations and Pohoata–Davies graphs), and that both types are necessary.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs and tree decompositions XVI. Complete bipartite induced minors
